First, for each item, we assessed the suitability for in-the-moment adaptation and mean factor loadings from four published articles. Three items with the highest overall factor loadings per SOC component (comprehensibility, manageability, meaningfulness) have been selected for our brief surveys. It is important to note that due to unacceptable fit indices obtained after fitting the three-factor SOC model on our data, we conducted our analyses using factor scores extracted from a unidimensional SOC model, which provided excellent fit indices (see Section 6)

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> In an exploratory study, we recruited a Hungarian sample of 98 individuals, comprising primarily university students entering via credit courses.

> For a pre-registered, confirmatory study (https://osf.io/2h5pc/), 297 participants have been recruited from the United States via Prolific, using the platform's representative sampling methodology.

> Participants of the representative U.S. sample enrolled through Prolific, and via university course forums in case of the Hungarian sample.

> Participants filled a short intake questionnaire where they were presented examples of the item pool.

> In addition, participants had the option to tailor their survey schedule to suit their routines by selecting the time they usually wake up.

> Participants provided basic demographic information and answered questions regarding their socioeconomic status, living arrangements, potential clinical diagnoses and, only in the representative U.S. sample, political affiliation.

> Furthermore, using the built in bot/LLM screening features provided by Qualtrics and Prolific, we inspected baseline survey submissions for suspicious participant behavior.

Ethics approval statement:

> Both studies were approved by the United Ethical Review Committee for Research in Psychology (EPKEB) 2025-131 (2025-056; 2024-13; 2021-38; 2020-40; 2019-29), and the authors complied with the Declaration of Helsinki.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p's > 0.1", Text = "None of the other individual differences were significantly related to overall levels of conspiracy mentality throughout the study (i.e. age, psychiatric diagnosis, education, subjective social status, locus of control; all p's > 0.1). to-day anxiety-reducing effect of conspiracy mentality in individuals without a psychiatric disorder (N = 3,083)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report:
Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1616 columns across 10 data files.
#### Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

42 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. **What this does not cover.** Only 8 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In an exploratory study, we recruited a Hungarian sample of 98 individuals, comprising primarily university students entering via credit courses.
For a pre-registered, confirmatory study (https://osf.io/2h5pc/), 297 participants have been recruited from the United States via Prolific, using the platform's representative sampling methodology.
Participants of the representative U.S. sample enrolled through Prolific, and via university course forums in case of the Hungarian sample.
Participants filled a short intake questionnaire where they were presented examples of the item pool.
In addition, participants had the option to tailor their survey schedule to suit their routines by selecting the time they usually wake up.

Participants provided basic demographic information and answered questions regarding their socioeconomic status, living arrangements, potential clinical diagnoses and, only in the representative U.S. sample, political affiliation.
Furthermore, using the built in bot/LLM screening features provided by Qualtrics and Prolific, we inspected baseline survey submissions for suspicious participant behavior.

report:
This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 16 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:16, File = c("01_cleaning_hun.Rmd",

metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 17 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `fit_brm_anx_conspi.rds`, `fit_brm_anx_conspi_x_iu.rds`, `fit_brm_anx_conspi_x_nfcc.rds`, `fit_brm_conspi_anx.rds`, `fit_brm_conspi_anx_x_iu.rds`, `fit_brm_conspi_anx_x_nfcc.rds`, `fit_brm_anx_conspi_tr.rds`, `fit_brm_anx_conspi_same.rds`, `fit_brm_soc_conspi.rds`, `fit_brm_soc_conspi_x_iu.rds`, `fit_brm_soc_conspi_x_nfcc.rds`, `fit_brm_conspi_soc.rds`, `fit_brm_conspi_soc_x_iu.rds`, `fit_brm_conspi_soc_x_nfcc.rds`, `fit_brm_soc_conspi_tr.rds`, `fit_brm_soc_conspi_same.rds`, `fit_brm_posaff_conspi_tr.rds`.
#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 16 scripts: 7 ran without error, 9 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

**Undefined-variable errors**
**2 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

text.text: Conspiracy theories are assumed to provide psychological relief, reducing anxiety and uncertainty in the short term, at the cost of longer-term harms.
Nevertheless, the temporal dynamics of conspiracy beliefs have rarely been investigated in naturalistic settings.

Here, we tested whether fluctuations in conspiracy mentality are associated with changes in anxiety and sense of coherence in everyday life, using experience sampling data collected in a Hungarian (N = 77, Nobs = 2,905) and a pre-registered representative U.S. sample (N = 200, Nobs = 10,609).

In both samples, we found moderate to strong evidence against a general association of conspiracy mentality with anxiety and sense of coherence across multiple timescales spanning from hours to weeks.

However, among older adults, increases in conspiracy mentality were followed by lower anxiety and a higher sense of coherence, while individuals reporting no psychiatric diagnosis also benefited in terms of reduced anxiety.

Together, these findings challenge the notion that conspiracy beliefs function as a universal buffer against anxiety and uncertainty, while the exploratory analyses point towards boundary conditions requiring further investigation.
Significance statement Conspiracy theories are thought to help people cope with anxiety and restore coherence, yet this assumption has rarely been tested on day-to-day timescales.

Using intensive longitudinal data collected in everyday life we found that while conspiracy mentality showed substantial fluctuations, these were unrelated to changes in anxiety or sense of coherence.
These findings held across multiple timescales in both a Hungarian and a representative U.S. sample.

In subgroups of older adults and people without a psychiatric diagnosis, however, increased conspiracy mentality was followed by reduced anxiety, whereas older individuals reported an increased sense of coherence.
These findings suggest that while conspiracy beliefs are not set in stone, they do not appear to function as a universal coping mechanism.

Do conspiracy theories help reduce anxiety and restore coherence?
Both popular and scientific accounts often assume that explaining a frightening world, even inaccurately, makes it feel less threatening and more comprehensible (1).

text.text: On this view, conspiracy belief works much like a cigarette -a hit of relief now, paid for in harm later (2) -serving epistemic and existential needs for certainty and meaning (1, 3).
text.formatted: On this view, conspiracy belief works much like a cigarette -a hit of relief now, paid for in harm later (2) -serving epistemic and existential needs for certainty and meaning <ref type="bibr">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr">3)</ref>.

text.text: This account is both intuitively appealing and theoretically plausible but remains almost entirely untested on the timescales at which such relief is presumed to occur: within hours and days of adopting conspiratorial explanations.
If conspiracy theories are embraced to alleviate anxiety and restore coherence, conspiracy mentality should fluctuate alongside changes in psychological states as individuals navigate everyday life.
Yet these dynamics remain largely unexamined in everyday life.
Here, we examine the malleability and the dynamics of conspiracy beliefs and their interplay with anxiety and coherence.
We test the relief hypothesis across two experience sampling studies, including a pre-registered study in a representative U.S. sample.
In times of heightened anxiety, individuals often turn to conspiracy theories to make sense of uncertain circumstances and restore coherence.
The adoption of such beliefs may serve epistemic motives, including the restoration of a sense of coherence (4).
text.formatted: The adoption of such beliefs may serve epistemic motives, including the restoration of a sense of coherence <ref type="bibr">(4)</ref>.

text.text: By attributing complex, apparently chaotic phenomena to powerful actors with identifiable motives, events may become comprehensible, predictable, and subjectively coherent (5).
text.formatted: By attributing complex, apparently chaotic phenomena to powerful actors with identifiable motives, events may become comprehensible, predictable, and subjectively coherent <ref type="bibr">(5)</ref>.

text.text: Such simplified causal explanations may also satisfy existential motives by helping individuals manage and reduce anxiety, at least temporarily (1, 4).
text.formatted: Such simplified causal explanations may also satisfy existential motives by helping individuals manage and reduce anxiety, at least temporarily <ref type="bibr">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr">4)</ref>.

text.text: If conspiracy beliefs reduce anxiety and restore coherence, the resulting relief could itself reinforce conspiracist thinking.
More broadly, this account aligns with the idea that inaccurate beliefs may nevertheless have utility -and hence persistbecause they are associated with positive internal outcomes (6, 7).
text.formatted: More broadly, this account aligns with the idea that inaccurate beliefs may nevertheless have utility -and hence persistbecause they are associated with positive internal outcomes <ref type="bibr">(6,</ref> <ref type="bibr">7)</ref>.

text.text: The proposed utility of endorsing conspiracy theories, however, remains to be demonstrated.
These effects might not be universal.
Individuals who find uncertainty aversive and value predictability and structure may be especially likely to turn to conspiracy theories and derive psychological benefit from them.
This proposition aligns with the well-established link between epistemic motives and conspiracy beliefs (4).
text.formatted: This proposition aligns with the well-established link between epistemic motives and conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr">(4)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, conspiracy mentality might reduce anxiety and restore a sense of coherence (5) especially in those with higher levels of intolerance of uncertainty (8).
text.formatted: Specifically, conspiracy mentality might reduce anxiety and restore a sense of coherence (5) especially in those with higher levels of intolerance of uncertainty <ref type="bibr">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, individuals with a higher need for cognitive closure tend to experience a stronger motivation to seek out explanations that establish order and reduce ambiguity (9).
text.formatted: Similarly, individuals with a higher need for cognitive closure tend to experience a stronger motivation to seek out explanations that establish order and reduce ambiguity <ref type="bibr">(9)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this reasoning, individuals with lower tolerance for uncertainty tend to adopt coping strategies that provide immediate relief, such as behavioral and cognitive avoidance (10, 11), a pattern mirroring the proposed short-term psychological benefits of conspiracy mentality.
text.formatted: In line with this reasoning, individuals with lower tolerance for uncertainty tend to adopt coping strategies that provide immediate relief, such as behavioral and cognitive avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11)</ref>, a pattern mirroring the proposed short-term psychological benefits of conspiracy mentality.

text.text: Emerging theories suggest that these benefits might be rather short-lived, and that adopting conspiracy beliefs may ultimately prove maladaptive in the long run (1, 2).
text.formatted: Emerging theories suggest that these benefits might be rather short-lived, and that adopting conspiracy beliefs may ultimately prove maladaptive in the long run <ref type="bibr">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr">2)</ref>.

text.text: While conspiracy beliefs may initially alleviate anxiety and restore coherence, they often reinforce chronic distrust, helplessness, and hypervigilance, thereby perpetuating anxiety and uncertainty over time.

Longitudinal and cross-sectional studies suggest that conspiracy beliefs are associated with slightly elevated stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms rather than genuine psychological recovery (12, 13), although relationships are generally modest in magnitude.
text.formatted: Longitudinal and cross-sectional studies suggest that conspiracy beliefs are associated with slightly elevated stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms rather than genuine psychological recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13)</ref>, although relationships are generally modest in magnitude.

text.text: Thus, "conspiracy beliefs may be psychologically rewarding in the short run; but perceivers and society pay a price for them in the long run" (van Prooijen, 2022, p5.).

In this sense, conspiracy thinking appears ultimately self-defeating, resembling avoidant coping strategies that provide temporary emotional regulation while undermining long-term resilience and adaptive problem-solving (14).
text.formatted: In this sense, conspiracy thinking appears ultimately self-defeating, resembling avoidant coping strategies that provide temporary emotional regulation while undermining long-term resilience and adaptive problem-solving <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: Despite strong theoretical claims, it remains unclear when these hypothesised short-term benefits affecting anxiety and coherence levels are realized, and when their long-term costs must be paid.
Critically, while this framework assumes that conspiracy beliefs are malleable, their day-to-day fluctuations have never been examined in everyday life.

Existing research has largely taken two approaches: examining longer-term associations using widely spaced longitudinal designs (12, 15), or demonstrating immediate effects of conspiracy primes in experimental settings (6, 16).
text.formatted: Existing research has largely taken two approaches: examining longer-term associations using widely spaced longitudinal designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15)</ref>, or demonstrating immediate effects of conspiracy primes in experimental settings <ref type="bibr">(6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, the short-term psychological consequences of conspiracy mentality in the naturalistic settings of daily life remain essentially untested.
Identifying the timescales on which these processes unfold is therefore crucial for understanding of the costs and benefits associated with conspiracy beliefs.
To address this gap, we use experience sampling to examine the malleability, the psychological dynamics and drivers of conspiracy beliefs.
We begin with establishing the malleability of conspiracy mentality.
We next evaluate whether individuals higher in conspiracy mentality report higher anxiety and lower sense of coherence overall.
Then, we turn to shorter-term benefits and test bidirectional day-to-day associations between anxiety, sense of coherence, and conspiracy mentality.

Specifically, we assess whether rises in anxiety and disruptions in sense of coherence predict subsequent increases in conspiracy mentality, and whether such thinking predicts subsequent reductions in anxiety and increases in sense of coherence.
We further test whether intolerance of uncertainty and need for closure amplify these associations.
Finally, we extend these analyses to within-day timescales and explore the more immediate psychological consequences of conspiracy mentality.
These analyses span two samples, including an exploratory study in a Hungarian sample, and a pre-registered confirmatory study in a representative U.S. sample.
First, we established a core assumption of the relief hypothesis: that conspiracy mentality is malleable.
Critically, day to day fluctuations in conspiracy mentality were substantial (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Critically, day to day fluctuations in conspiracy mentality were substantial (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Across two experience sampling studies lasting about 2-3 weeks each, 43 and 41% (in the representative U.S. and the Hungarian samples, respectively) of variance in a conspiracy mentality latent variable was not explained by individual tendencies that persisted during the study period (ICC = 57/59%).
The extent of fluctuations was comparable to that of anxiety (ICC = 67/62%) and a sense of coherence (ICC = 56/51%).

Importantly, fluctuations in conspiracy mentality were reliably measured (α = 0.67/0.72, avg. loading = 0.55 in multilevel confirmatory factor models that had excellent fit, see Table S4, S5 and S6 in Supplementary Materials), underscoring that the changes can not be solely attributed to measurement noise.
text.formatted: Importantly, fluctuations in conspiracy mentality were reliably measured (α = 0.67/0.72, avg. loading = 0.55 in multilevel confirmatory factor models that had excellent fit, see Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>, S5 and S6 in Supplementary Materials), underscoring that the changes can not be solely attributed to measurement noise.

text.text: As a follow-up, we explored how universal the malleability of conspiracy mentality was.
We observed significant age-related differences in the within-individual variability (i.e. standard deviation) of conspiracy mentality.

Specifically, conspiracy beliefs were significantly less stable in younger individuals, whereas older individuals showed lower within-person variability in their beliefs (β = -0.21, [-0.44,-0.15], p < 0.001).

text.text: None of the other demographic or personality variables we considered were related to within-person variability in conspiracy mentality (see the related description and Table S2 in Supplementary Materials).

text.text: We argued that conspiracy mentality is ultimately self-defeating, despite its short-term benefits.
We expected that higher average conspiracy mentality throughout the study periods would be associated with higher anxiety and lower coherence levels.
However, no significant association was found neither in the exploratory nor the confirmatory study.

Higher conspiracy mentality did not predict overall higher anxiety (representative U.S.: β = 0.06 [-0.07,018], p = 0.375, BF01 = 2.90, p(β>0) = 84.25%; Hungarian: β = 0.18, [-0.01,0.36], p = 0.058, BF01 = 0.63, p(β>0) = 96.03%; 95% confidence intervals in square brackets) or lower coherence levels (representative U.S.: β = -0.06, [-0.18,0.06], p = 0.302, BF01 = 2.70, p(β<0) = 85.51%; Hungarian: β = -0.10, [-0.29,0.08], p = 0.262, BF01 = 1.58, p(β<0) = 84.65%).

text.text: To conclude, our data does not imply any psychological costs of conspiracy mentality over 2-3 weeks.
Next, we evaluated whether conspiracy mentality yields any short-term benefits in terms of providing relief from aversive psychological states.
Therefore, we tested whether day-to-day changes in anxiety and coherence are followed by changes in conspiracy mentality, and vice versa.

As we reasoned that conspiracy mentality might function as a coping mechanism, we expected that an increase in anxiety levels and a decrease in coherence would be followed by an increase in conspiracy mentality on the next day.
However, the data provided no support for these hypotheses.

The level of conspiracy mentality was not predicted by anxiety (representative U. However, one may argue that the benefits may emerge over a much shorter timescale, with the associated costs also occurring relatively soon thereafter.
We therefore shifted our focus to the within-day course of anxiety and coherence, asking whether both the putative benefits and the costs of conspiracy mentality emerge over narrower time windows.

We hypothesised that conspiracy mentality would be associated with lower anxiety and increased sense of coherence earlier in the day, while towards the end of the day, it would predict higher anxiety and lower coherence.

Yet again, we found no significant associations between changes in conspiracy mentality and anxiety (representative U.S.: β = 0.01, [-0.01,0.03], p = 0.474, BF01 = 4.29, p(β>0) = 77.83%; Hungarian: β = 0.02, [-0.01,0.05], p = 0.418, BF01 = 1.52, p(β>0) = 91.10%) or coherence (representative U.S.: β = -0.01, [-0.03,0.00], p = 0.143, BF01 = 1.78, p(β<0) = 93.71%; Hungarian: β = -0.00, [-0.04,0.03], p = 0.799, BF01 = 3.31, p(β<0) = 65.28%).

In all, the short-lived anxiety-reducing or coherence-restoring benefits of conspiracy mentality, followed by psychological harm soon after, could not be established in the course of a single day.
Lastly, we performed exploratory analyses to test whether the short-term benefits of conspiracy mentality could arrive on an even shorter timescale.
Specifically, we tested whether momentary conspiracy mentality predicted lower concurrent anxiety and higher concurrent coherence.

text.text: Next, we tested whether the proposed benefits of conspiracy belief occur only in those individuals who find uncertainty and lack of structure more aversive.
However, we found no support for the moderation of the above associations by intolerance of uncertainty and need for closure.
The pre-registered hypotheses concentrated on day-to-day associations.

Individuals less tolerant of uncertainty did not turn to conspiracy theories the day after their anxiety increased (representative U. Lastly, we explored whether longer-term costs of conspiracy mentality were predicted by intolerance of uncertainty.

However, such individual differences did not moderate the association between study-period averages of conspiracy mentality and anxiety (representative U.S.: β = -0.05, [-0.15,0.05], p = 0.360, BF01 = 1.35, p(β<0) = 77.83%; Hungarian: β = -0.04, [-0.33,0.24], p = 0.764, BF01 = 2.35, p(β<0) = 57.19%) or coherence (representative U.S.: β = 0.02, [-0.26,0.30], p = 0.879, BF01 = 1.24, p(β>0) = 79.04%; Hungarian: β = 0.02, [-0.26,0.30], p = 0.879, BF01 = 2.19, p(β>0) = 55.76%).

text.text: Similarly, between-person differences in need for closure did not moderate the associations in either samples (see Supplementary Materials).

Having evaluated the pre-registered hypotheses, we turned to explore the potential boundary conditions of the posited calming effects of conspiracy mentality in the larger, representative U.S. sample.
Multiple boundary conditions emerged.
Age moderated the association between yesterday's conspiracy mentality and today's anxiety (β = -0.02, [-0.05,-0.00], p = 0.048, BF01 = 1.16, p(β<0) = 96.64%).

text.text: Examination of marginal effects revealed that older individuals demonstrated a decrease in anxiety the day after their conspiracy mentality increased (Figure 3A).

text.text: Similarly, in participants who did not report any psychiatric disorders, higher conspiracy mentality was followed by reduced anxiety on the subsequent day (β = -0.05, [-0.11,-0.00], p = 0.041, BF01 = 0.42, p(β<0) = 97.71%; Figure 3B).

text.text: Age also moderated the association between conspiracy mentality and coherence the day after (β = 0.04, [0.01,0.07], p = 0.008, BF01 = 0.48, p(β>0) = 98.49%; Figure 3C).

text.text: Inspection of marginal effects indicated that, in older individuals, higher conspiracy mentality predicted an increase in coherence on the following day.
Such age related differences imply that older individuals derive greater benefits from endorsing conspiracy theories.
Analyses of further boundary conditions are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
Lastly, we asked whether more enduring tendencies to endorse conspiracy beliefs were related to the individual differences considered above.

We found that individuals less tolerant of uncertainty reported an overall greater endorsement of conspiracy theories throughout the study period (β = 0.20, [0.07,0.33], p = 0.003), suggesting that individuals finding uncertainty more aversive are more likely to endorse conspiracy beliefs in general.
Similarly, a higher need for cognitive closure predicted increased conspiracy mentality throughout the study period (β = 0.15, [0.03,0.27], p = 0.016).

Conspiracy beliefs are often portrayed as a psychological cigarette: a brief dose of relief whose longer-term costs are ultimately paid through maladaptive coping (1, 2).
text.formatted: Conspiracy beliefs are often portrayed as a psychological cigarette: a brief dose of relief whose longer-term costs are ultimately paid through maladaptive coping <ref type="bibr">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr">2)</ref>.

text.text: First, we observed substantial day-to-day malleability in conspiracy mentality.
Strikingly, its fluctuations were comparable in magnitude to those of anxiety, a psychological state long known to vary substantially within individuals.

Although such malleability is a prerequisite for any dynamic regulatory function, we found little evidence that conspiracy mentality generally provides psychological relief or contributes to psychological harm.

Across study-period averages, day-to-day lags, within-day trajectories, and momentary associations, conspiracy mentality was neither reliably preceded by heightened anxiety or reduced coherence, nor followed by improvements in either.
Bayesian analyses generally provided moderate-to-strong evidence in favor of the absence of these associations.

Taken together, convergent findings across two naturalistic experience-sampling studies, including a pre-registered representative U.S. sample, challenge the notion that conspiracy beliefs function as a universal source of psychological relief in everyday life.
Why, then, do previous studies frequently report associations between psychological distress and conspiracy belief?
One possibility is that relationships observed between individuals do not necessarily generalize to processes unfolding within individuals over time.
The present findings suggest that it depends on the level of analysis and boundary conditions.
Cross-sectional data provides snapshots that seemingly allow inference at the between-individual level yet may mask within-individual fluctuations (17).
text.formatted: Cross-sectional data provides snapshots that seemingly allow inference at the between-individual level yet may mask within-individual fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref>.

text.text: These inferences, however, may not always generalize to intra-individual characteristics and processes (18).
text.formatted: These inferences, however, may not always generalize to intra-individual characteristics and processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: The processes unfolding within the same person in their daily lives, such as the temporal dynamics between conspiracy belief and anxiety can only be explored using time-series data with high ecological validity (19).
text.formatted: The processes unfolding within the same person in their daily lives, such as the temporal dynamics between conspiracy belief and anxiety can only be explored using time-series data with high ecological validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: Highlighting the malleability of conspiracy mentality, our unique naturalistic time-series data revealed substantial and systematic within-person variability in conspiracy beliefs.
Remarkably, approximately 40% of the variance in conspiracy mentality occurred within individuals, a proportion comparable to that observed for state anxiety.
The strong psychometric properties of the measure further suggest that this variability cannot be reduced to measurement error.
These findings suggest that conspiracy mentality is more dynamic than is often assumed and cannot be understood solely as a stable individual disposition.

Even though there is a strong theoretical basis to expect that these fluctuations may reflect mechanisms aimed at reducing anxiety and restoring coherence, our results suggest that day-to-day changes in conspiracy mentality could not be explained by preceding increases in anxiety or drops in coherence.
This conclusion remained unchanged after exploring subgroups and boundary conditions.
Theoretically, the central puzzle is what explains substantial fluctuations in conspiracy mentality.

First, general anxiety might not be specific enough: it can originate in countless personal circumstances that have little relevance to conspiratorial explanations, whereas uncertainty surrounding threatening public events or the intentions of powerful actors may exhibit more immediate dynamics with conspiracy mentality (but also see 13, 16).
text.formatted: First, general anxiety might not be specific enough: it can originate in countless personal circumstances that have little relevance to conspiratorial explanations, whereas uncertainty surrounding threatening public events or the intentions of powerful actors may exhibit more immediate dynamics with conspiracy mentality (but also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, intolerance of uncertainty predicted higher levels of conspiracy mentality, suggesting that being anxious when facing uncertainty might be more specifically related to conspiracy mentality.
Second, the primary benefits of conspiracy belief might be self-evaluative rather than directly anxiety-related.

Conspiracy narratives may protect fragile or unstable self-perceptions by allowing believers to experience themselves as unusually perceptive, knowledgeable, or resistant to manipulation (2) -without necessarily reducing their momentary levels of anxiety.
Consequently, any emotional relief might be indirect, mediated by restored epistemic status, self-esteem, or individual and collective narcissistic needs.
Indeed, individuals with a contingent self-esteem may derive greater utility from the momentary adoption of conspiracy beliefs (7, 20).
text.formatted: Indeed, individuals with a contingent self-esteem may derive greater utility from the momentary adoption of conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr">(7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, although this study provides evidence against a generic relief hypothesis, it leaves more specific ego-defensive accounts to be tested in everyday life.
While we found evidence against universal psychological benefits of conspiracy mentality, exploratory analyses hinted that certain individuals might enjoy relief.

On a day-to-day level, elevated conspiracy mentality predicted lower subsequent anxiety among older adults and participants without a reported psychiatric diagnosis, while older adults -whose conspiracy mentality was less malleable -also experienced increased coherence.
One possibility is that as the psychological function of conspiracy beliefs changes across the lifespan, reliance on them in coping with anxiety and uncertainty might also become more rewarding.
This, however, seems somewhat counterintuitive in light of the hypothesised long-term harms caused by conspiracy beliefs (1).
However, short-term benefits and long-term costs are not necessarily mutually exclusive over a lifespan either.
Furthermore, we found that elevated conspiracy mentality was followed by reduced anxiety in those without a psychiatric disorder.
In those who report having a psychiatric diagnosis, anxiety might be more pervasive, or have causes that are unaffected by endorsing conspiracy mentality.
However, future studies should confirm these exploratory findings and test the underlying mechanisms.

A key strength of this study is that it tested pre-registered hypotheses in a representative U.S. sample that was assessed during a politically turbulent period, providing room for conspiratorial ideation.
On the other hand, the limitations of the study point towards future directions.
First, it is possible that the broad conspiracy mentality we assessed here fluctuates for different reasons than specific conspiracy narratives linked to concrete events.

Future research should combine event-contingent assessments including specific and open-ended measures of conspiracy mentality with real-time measures of media exposure, search behaviour, and social interaction.
Furthermore, the repeated assessment of conspiratorial ideas might itself have increased their accessibility or endorsement, potentially interfering with the naturalistic dynamics of such thoughts.
However, in our datasets, conspiracy mentality did not increase linearly as people spent more days in the study.

While the complexity of the models and the number of exploratory moderators might increase the risk of false positives and negatives, our confirmatory study was preregistered, and we interpreted the exploratory results cautiously, while giving larger weight to the preregistered effects.
Finally, the relevant processes may unfold more gradually than the investigated timescales allowed.
Repeated uncertainty, identity threat, or algorithmically personalized exposure might need to accumulate before producing detectable changes in conspiracy mentality.
Future research should therefore examine longer temporal windows.

Furthermore, to fully appreciate the intricacies of conspiracy beliefs, they might need to be considered as socially embedded phenomena, shaped not only by the demand to reduce anxiety and restore coherence, but also by interpersonal reinforcement, maintenance of self-esteem, social affiliation, and personalized information environments.

text.text: In an exploratory study, we recruited a Hungarian sample of 98 individuals, comprising primarily university students entering via credit courses.
For a pre-registered, confirmatory study (https://osf.io/2h5pc/), 297 participants have been recruited from the United States via Prolific, using the platform's representative sampling methodology.

text.text: Beyond the standard inclusion of gender, age and ethnicity, we extended our representativity criteria to political affiliation.

Both studies were approved by the United Ethical Review Committee for Research in Psychology (EPKEB) 2025-131 (2025-056; 2024-13; 2021-38; 2020-40; 2019-29), and the authors complied with the Declaration of Helsinki.

To retain only high quality data for the analyses of both datasets, we applied several well established and pre-registered (in the representative U.S. sample) quality criteria both at the individual and beep levels.
We made inferences on data quality primarily based on completion speeds, attention checks and compliance levels in the experience sampling phases.
Our detailed data quality control process can be found in the Supplementary Materials.

Design.
Participants of the representative U.S. sample enrolled through Prolific, and via university course forums in case of the Hungarian sample.
In both cases, individuals first completed a cross-sectional survey via Qualtrics.
After doing so, participants joined the intensive longitudinal sampling phase, hosted on m-Path (21).
text.formatted: After doing so, participants joined the intensive longitudinal sampling phase, hosted on m-Path <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref>.

text.text: Participants filled a short intake questionnaire where they were presented examples of the item pool.
In addition, participants had the option to tailor their survey schedule to suit their routines by selecting the time they usually wake up.

Following intake, participants received brief assessment surveys four times a day for 15 days in the Hungarian sample and for 20 days in the representative sample in order to obtain a sufficient number of observations per person to model within-individual associations at the day-to-day level (22).
text.formatted: Following intake, participants received brief assessment surveys four times a day for 15 days in the Hungarian sample and for 20 days in the representative sample in order to obtain a sufficient number of observations per person to model within-individual associations at the day-to-day level <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref>.

text.text: Participants received four beeps a day, emitted semi-randomly approximately four hours apart within 30-minute windows.
The emission of each notification was followed by a reminder 10 minutes later, with the surveys expiring another 10 minutes later.
Anxiety and sense of coherence were measured in every questionnaire.
Conspiracy mentality was assessed only on the given day's first questionnaire participants responded to, as we expected no meaningful within-day variability.
On average, surveys took no longer than one minute to complete.
However, each day's first completed beep was slightly longer, due to the inclusion of the conspiracy mentality items.

After the conclusion of the 15/20 day sampling regimes, participants in the U.S. sample have received monetary rewards, whereas students in the Hungarian sample received course credits as compensation, both proportionate to the number of surveys they completed (for a detailed description of incentive systems see Supplementary Materials).
Measurements.
Cross-sectional phase.

Participants provided basic demographic information and answered questions regarding their socioeconomic status, living arrangements, potential clinical diagnoses and, only in the representative U.S. sample, political affiliation.
Subsequently, they completed several trait-level questionnaires.

Analyses.
All analyses were performed with R 4.5.2 in RStudio 2026.8.1.195.
In the representative U.S.

sample, the data quality checks yielded a total sample size of N = 200, Ndays = 3,083 and Nobs = 10,609 (day-level mean compliance = 87.7%), whereas the Hungarian dataset contained N = 77, Ndays = 847 and Nobs = 2,905 (day-level mean compliance = 62.1%), which were analysed separately.
In order to test our hypotheses, we fitted linear mixed effects models using the lmer function from the lme4 package in R (33).
text.formatted: In order to test our hypotheses, we fitted linear mixed effects models using the lmer function from the lme4 package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33)</ref>.

text.text: To estimate the hypothesised temporal associations and moderation effects, we first calculated latent factor scores using CFA and mlCFA for the baseline and ESM measures, respectively.
Fit indices were satisfactory or excellent for all latent variables (see Table S4 in Supplementary Materials), with the exception of the NFC scale.
text.formatted: Fit indices were satisfactory or excellent for all latent variables (see Table <ref type="table">S4</ref> in Supplementary Materials), with the exception of the NFC scale.

text.text: The model structure showed an unacceptable fit, and as a result we computed a composite score to use for our analyses, in line with our pre-registered strategy.
Subsequently, baseline scores have been centered within their respective samples using the grand mean.
In case of the ESM measures, both within-and between-individual variance has been extracted from the factor scores, centered within the samples and individuals, respectively.
To estimate day-to-day associations with conspiracy mentality, measured once a day, daily individual-specific means for anxiety and coherence have been computed.
Furthermore, first-order time lagged versions of conspiracy mentality, anxiety and coherence have been computed on the day level.
Overall, we sought to test associations between conspiracy mentality, anxiety and coherence across four timescales.

These included effects pertaining to the global self-report (trait) measures, person level study-period averages, day-to-day associations, within-day trajectories and associations within a single moment.
To test these assumptions, we fitted pre-registered linear mixed models for the study-period average and day-to-day hypotheses, and fitted exploratory models for the within-day and momentary tests.
The hypothesised moderator variables have been entered after testing the base models.

While models varied in both their fixed and random effect structures, the control variables of age, gender, number of days spent in the study and weekend (as a dichotomous variable) have been entered as fixed effects in all models.
To test the effects of exploratory moderators, we fitted models identical to day-to-day models described above, with each moderator tested separately.
The study-period average and day-to-day associations were tested using the same model.
The outcome variables were daily means of anxiety and coherence, in their respective models.
As key predictors, we included yesterday's within-person centered and study-period average scores of conspiracy mentality.

To test predictions of yesterday's anxiety and coherence on today's conspiracy mentality, the within-individual outcome and predictor variables were switched, while also controlling for study-period averages of conspiracy mentality.
To further control for potential confounding effects, we included the day's first assessment scores of anxiety and coherence, coinciding with conspiracy mentality measurements.
In both model types, yesterday's within-individual scores of the outcome variable were entered to account for autocorrelation effects.
To estimate daily trajectories, the outcome variables were within-day observations of anxiety and coherence, as measured on occasions subsequent to the daily conspiracy mentality observation.
The key predictor was the interaction term of daily conspiracy mentality and the number of surveys sent since the day's first completed survey.

Control variables included study-period average scores of conspiracy mentality, to adjust for longer-lasting associations, and the day's first observations of anxiety and coherence, to adjust for baseline differences on a given day.
The models estimating momentary associations included the first daily observations of anxiety and coherence.
Daily conspiracy mentality was entered as the key predictor, while the models also controlled for autocorrelation effects and study-period average conspiracy mentality.
To account for individual differences in all models, random intercepts were used in each model.
Random slopes were included for the key predictors, the autocorrelation effects and the daily first assessment scores, where applicable (see Supplementary Materials).
When models failed to converge, we first aimed to identify optimizers that facilitated convergence.
In case of optimizer failure, we removed random effect correlations, as they were unrelated to our hypotheses.
Two example models can be seen in Equation 1.

After fitting the pre-registered frequentist linear mixed-effect models, we fitted Bayesian regression models to make inferences on our ability to draw conclusions regarding the associations observed on the four timescales.

Informative priors for main effects were set by using normal distributions (mean = 0, SD = 0.3) that appeared to correspond to a reasonable magnitude of time-lagged cross-construct associations in daily life research.

To retain only high quality data for the analyses, we applied several well established and preregistered (in representative U.S.) criteria both at the individual and beep levels.
On the individual level, we first calculated a relative speed index (RSI) for all baseline cross-sectional survey submissions.
Individuals scoring above 2.0 had their baseline data removed from our analyses (1).
Furthermore, using the built in bot/LLM screening features provided by Qualtrics and Prolific, we inspected baseline survey submissions for suspicious participant behavior.

For the representative U.S. sample only, participants who failed both attention check items embedded in the cross-sectional survey had their submissions aborted automatically, making them ineligible for both rewards and the option to participate in the ESM phase.
Lastly, participants completing less than 33% percent of all available ESM surveys have been excluded from analyses due to insufficient amount of data for the modelling of day-to-day effects (2).
Beep level quality control measures have been identical in both studies.
Software related anomalies have been filtered from the dataset (e.g. timing misalignments, duplicated beeps).

Failed attention checks in the ESM surveys (see Intensive longitudinal sampling phase), as well as an average response time of less than 650ms per item (Geeraerts & Kuppens, 2020), resulted in the exclusion of the corresponding beep from the analyses.

Given the heterogeneity of the representative U.S. sample, we explored whether the malleability of conspiracy mentality and the relief it is proposed to yield have any boundary conditions.
First, we considered age, given the rich variability in the sample and known age-related differences in both conspiracy mentality (3) and emotion regulation (4).
Second, we hypothesised that individuals who report having received a psychiatric diagnosis might have qualitatively different coping mechanisms compared to healthy participants.
Third, given the robust links between socio-economic status and conspiracist tendencies (5), both the level of education and subjective social status have been included.
Finally, we considered locus of control as lack of perceived control might specifically predict conspiracist tendencies (6).
text.formatted: Finally, we considered locus of control as lack of perceived control might specifically predict conspiracist tendencies <ref type="bibr">(6)</ref>.

text.text: Then, we also explored whether these factors predicted the malleability or the overall level of conspiracy mentality.
The malleability of conspiracy mentality (defined as the within-person SD) was significantly predicted by age, but was not significantly associated with any of the other moderators.
The association with age is presented in the main text, and the full regression summary is shown below.

Regarding the relief hypothesis, age and self-reported psychiatric diagnosis emerged as significant moderators of the association of conspiracy mentality with anxiety and sense of coherence the day after.
These results are reported in the main text.
Curiously, in a small subgroup of seven individuals without a high school diploma, yesterday's anxiety levels were positively associated with today's conspiracy mentality.
Given the small subsample driving this exploratory finding, we refrain from drawing any conclusions and recommend further replication.

Subjective social status and locus of control did not moderate the associations in the U.S. sample, whereas in the Hungarian sample, no significant moderation effect was found regarding either of the proposed constructs.

text.text: First, we revisited handling convergence issues.

Specifically, we adopted the following procedure: • As a standard approach, we used the bobyqa optimizer to support convergence across models • Whenever convergence failed, we first ran allFit() from the lme4 package to identify optimizers capable of handling convergence issues.
The most frequently used optimizers were nlminbwrap and nloptwrap • If no optimizer succeeded, we removed the correlation terms of random effects, as they fell outside the focus of our analyses.

This final remedy lead to convergence in all cases where optimizers failed Reason: we encountered more convergence issues than we had expected at the preregistration phase and became aware of more recent best practice recommendations in the meantime (7).
text.formatted: This final remedy lead to convergence in all cases where optimizers failed Reason: we encountered more convergence issues than we had expected at the preregistration phase and became aware of more recent best practice recommendations in the meantime <ref type="bibr">(7)</ref>.

text.text: As compared to the pre-registered analytical plan, this approach let us retain more random slopes in the model, which were critical for reliable fixed-effects inference.

In addition, to test whether Intolerance of Uncertainty or Need for Closure moderated the associations between Conspiracy Mentality and Anxiety or Sense of Coherence over a longer timescale, the preregistered models were extended with interaction terms at the between-person level.
Specifically, we tested whether the above personality constructs moderated the associations between study-period averages of anxiety, sense of coherence, and conspiracy mentality.

Reason: the preregistered moderation hypotheses concerned associations in terms of the within-person variance component, which are little influenced by estimating an interaction at the between-person level.
Therefore, for the sake of simplicity, we decided to extend these models, instead of fitting separate models estimating the interaction only at the between-person level.

Finally, the preregistration included hypotheses regarding within-day dynamics of positive affect as a function of conspiracy mentality, but in the manuscript we report within-day dynamics of anxiety.
Reason: ensure consistency of the outcomes across the various timescales we considered.

Then, we examined whether conspiracy mentality provides relief on the following day.

Changes in conspiracy mentality were not associated with neither subsequent anxiety (representative U.S.: β = -0.01, [-0.03,0.01], p = 0.242 , BF01 = 11.51, p(β<0) = 85.64%; Hungarian: β = 0.01, [-0.05,0.06], p = 0.902, BF01 = 9.23, p(β>0) = 54.20%) nor coherence levels (representative U.S.: β = 0.00, [-0.03,0.03], p = 0.978, BF01 = 17.96, p(β>0) = 53.94%; Hungarian: β = -0.01, [-0.06,0.04], p = 0.697, BF01 = 7.73, p(β<0) = 58.01%).

text.text: Notably, Bayesian analyses indicated moderate to strong evidence for the lack of association.

Thus, from one day to the other, conspiracy mentality does not seem to be predicted by anxiety or sense of coherence or to yield any benefits neither in terms of reducing anxiety nor restoring coherence either.
Bayesian analyses indicated moderate evidence for the lack of associations.

text.text: Beep and day level compliance rates across the two samples.

In the representative U.S. sample, average beep-level compliance rate was 66.31% (median = 75%, SD = 25.84, min = 10%, max = 100%), while the day-level compliance was 87.65% (median = 100%, SD = 19.76 , min = 35%, max = 100%).

In the case of the Hungarian sample, mean beep-level compliance was 45.08% (median = 51.25%, SD = 19.78, min = 6.25%, max = 71.25%), with daylevel compliance reaching an average of 62.1% (median = 75%, SD = 17.95, min = 25%, max = 75%).

Items selection rationale and in-the-moment adaptation of the SOC-13 scale To adapt the SOC-13 scale (8) to ecological momentary assessment, we followed theoretical and empirical considerations. First, for each item, we assessed the suitability for in-the-moment adaptation and mean factor loadings from four published articles. Three items with the highest overall factor loadings per SOC component (comprehensibility, manageability, meaningfulness) have been selected for our brief surveys. It is important to note that due to unacceptable fit indices obtained after fitting the three-factor SOC model on our data, we conducted our analyses using factor scores extracted from a unidimensional SOC model, which provided excellent fit indices (see Section 6). Such empirical shortcomings of the factor structure of the SOC-13 are widely documented in cross-sectional studies as well (9). References
